lessons.title: File permissions
lessons.summary: The group can read but not write the file.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Directory search permission is needed to traverse a path.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A teammate belongs to the file group but cannot open a file under a private parent directory. Inspect permissions on every parent directory.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: The group can execute the file. This is not a sound assumption; the group can read but not write the file.

lessons.takeaway: Directory search permission is needed to traverse a path.

lessons.title: Ownership
lessons.summary: It changes the owning user or group.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Ownership and permission bits are separate controls.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A service running as app cannot read a root-owned configuration with mode 600. Check the service identity and grant narrowly scoped read access.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: It changes the file content encoding. This is not a sound assumption; it changes the owning user or group.

lessons.takeaway: Ownership and permission bits are separate controls.

lessons.title: Symbolic links
lessons.summary: It stores a path to another filesystem object.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A symlink can become dangling when its target is removed.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A deployment symlink points to a release directory that was removed. Inspect the link target and restore or repoint it to a valid release.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: It must share the target inode. This is not a sound assumption; it stores a path to another filesystem object.

lessons.takeaway: A symlink can become dangling when its target is removed.

lessons.title: Hard links
lessons.summary: Both directory entries reference the same inode.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Removing one hard link does not delete data while another link remains.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: Removing a filename does not reclaim the expected space and another hard link exists. Inspect the inode link count and remaining directory entries.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Each link contains an independent data copy. This is not a sound assumption; both directory entries reference the same inode.

lessons.takeaway: Removing one hard link does not delete data while another link remains.

lessons.title: Pipelines
lessons.summary: The first command's standard output to the next command's standard input.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Standard error is not included unless redirected.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A command reports errors on the terminal but the downstream parser receives none. Check which output stream carries the messages.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: It automatically merges all standard error streams. This is not a sound assumption; the first command's standard output to the next command's standard input.

lessons.takeaway: Standard error is not included unless redirected.

lessons.title: Quoting
lessons.summary: Quoting prevents word splitting and pathname expansion on that value.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Untrusted values should be passed as data rather than evaluated as shell code.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A cleanup script fails on filenames containing spaces. Quote expansions and test with representative filenames in a safe directory.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Quoting executes the variable as a command. This is not a sound assumption; quoting prevents word splitting and pathname expansion on that value.

lessons.takeaway: Untrusted values should be passed as data rather than evaluated as shell code.

lessons.title: Processes
lessons.summary: A currently running process within a PID namespace.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: PIDs may be reused after processes exit.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A saved PID now belongs to a different process than yesterday. Verify process identity and start time before sending a signal.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: A PID is a globally permanent machine identifier. This is not a sound assumption; a currently running process within a PID namespace.

lessons.takeaway: PIDs may be reused after processes exit.

lessons.title: Signals
lessons.summary: SIGTERM asks a process to terminate and may be handled.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: SIGKILL cannot be caught for application cleanup.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A service needs time to flush buffered work during shutdown. Send a graceful stop and wait for a bounded shutdown period.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: SIGKILL guarantees application cleanup completes. This is not a sound assumption; sIGTERM asks a process to terminate and may be handled.

lessons.takeaway: SIGKILL cannot be caught for application cleanup.

lessons.title: Disk blocks
lessons.summary: Space allocation for mounted filesystems.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Filesystem usage and directory usage can differ for open deleted files.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: df shows a full filesystem but du finds much less visible file data. Look for deleted files still held open by processes.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: It reports only the sizes of visible files in one directory. This is not a sound assumption; space allocation for mounted filesystems.

lessons.takeaway: Filesystem usage and directory usage can differ for open deleted files.

lessons.title: Inodes
lessons.summary: Creation of new filesystem objects.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Many tiny files can exhaust inodes before byte capacity.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A filesystem has free gigabytes but creating a new file fails with no space. Check inode usage and locate excessive small-file growth.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: It only prevents existing files from being read. This is not a sound assumption; creation of new filesystem objects.

lessons.takeaway: Many tiny files can exhaust inodes before byte capacity.

lessons.title: Open file limits
lessons.summary: The number of file descriptors a process can hold open.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Sockets also consume file descriptors.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A service logs too many open files while disk space remains healthy. Inspect descriptor usage and the service limit for leaks or legitimate demand.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: It limits only the number of directory entries on disk. This is not a sound assumption; the number of file descriptors a process can hold open.

lessons.takeaway: Sockets also consume file descriptors.

lessons.title: Load average
lessons.summary: Tasks in uninterruptible sleep can contribute.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: High load does not by itself prove CPU saturation.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: Load rises sharply while CPU utilization remains low and storage is slow. Inspect task states and storage latency alongside CPU metrics.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Load average measures only CPU percentage. This is not a sound assumption; tasks in uninterruptible sleep can contribute.

lessons.takeaway: High load does not by itself prove CPU saturation.

lessons.title: Memory cache
lessons.summary: Unused RAM is often used for reclaimable filesystem cache.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Available memory is more useful than free memory alone for capacity triage.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A host shows low free RAM but high available RAM and no memory pressure. Check available memory and pressure before declaring a leak.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: All cached memory is permanently unavailable to applications. This is not a sound assumption; unused RAM is often used for reclaimable filesystem cache.

lessons.takeaway: Available memory is more useful than free memory alone for capacity triage.

lessons.title: OOM evidence
lessons.summary: Kernel logs and the relevant cgroup memory events.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A container memory limit can be reached while the host still has free RAM.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A container exits with 137 after a deployment. Correlate termination details with memory events and resource limits.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Every exit code 137 proves a kernel OOM kill. This is not a sound assumption; kernel logs and the relevant cgroup memory events.

lessons.takeaway: A container memory limit can be reached while the host still has free RAM.

lessons.title: Socket inspection
lessons.summary: Listening TCP sockets using numeric addresses.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A listener bound to loopback is not directly reachable through the host's external address.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: An application responds locally but not from another host. Check the listener address and port before investigating the network path.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: It proves every firewall permits the port. This is not a sound assumption; listening TCP sockets using numeric addresses.

lessons.takeaway: A listener bound to loopback is not directly reachable through the host's external address.

lessons.title: Name resolution
lessons.summary: getent follows the configured name service lookup path.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Local host entries and resolver configuration can affect application resolution.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A name resolves with a DNS tool but the application gets a different address. Compare the application's resolution path with NSS and local host configuration.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: getent always bypasses local host entries. This is not a sound assumption; getent follows the configured name service lookup path.

lessons.takeaway: Local host entries and resolver configuration can affect application resolution.

lessons.title: Mount options
lessons.summary: Writes through that mounted filesystem view.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Mount flags can deny writes even when file mode bits allow them.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: Writes fail with read-only filesystem after storage errors. Inspect mount state and kernel storage errors before attempting recovery.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Root can always write through a read-only mount. This is not a sound assumption; writes through that mounted filesystem view.

lessons.takeaway: Mount flags can deny writes even when file mode bits allow them.

lessons.title: Deleted executables
lessons.summary: The process retains references to the mapped executable data.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Updating an executable on disk does not automatically restart every running process.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A security update replaces a binary but an old process is still running. Identify affected processes and schedule controlled restarts.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Removing the pathname immediately terminates every process using it. This is not a sound assumption; the process retains references to the mapped executable data.

lessons.takeaway: Updating an executable on disk does not automatically restart every running process.

lessons.title: Zombies
lessons.summary: An exited child whose termination status has not been reaped.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The parent normally reaps child status with a wait operation.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A service parent accumulates many zombie children. Inspect the parent and correct its child reaping behavior.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: It is a process using all available CPU. This is not a sound assumption; an exited child whose termination status has not been reaped.

lessons.takeaway: The parent normally reaps child status with a wait operation.

lessons.title: System calls
lessons.summary: System calls and signals observed for a traced process.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Tracing can add overhead and expose sensitive argument data.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A process hangs while opening a path and logs provide little detail. Use a scoped trace with appropriate permissions and inspect blocking calls.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: It always reconstructs high-level application source code. This is not a sound assumption; system calls and signals observed for a traced process.

lessons.takeaway: Tracing can add overhead and expose sensitive argument data.

lessons.title: Scheduling priority
lessons.summary: Lower scheduling priority relative to competing normal tasks.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Nice values do not impose a hard CPU usage ceiling.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A batch job interferes with latency-sensitive work on a shared host. Evaluate scheduling priority and resource controls for the batch workload.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: A higher nice value guarantees more CPU time. This is not a sound assumption; lower scheduling priority relative to competing normal tasks.

lessons.takeaway: Nice values do not impose a hard CPU usage ceiling.

lessons.title: Swap pressure
lessons.summary: Memory pressure requiring closer investigation.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Swap activity should be correlated with latency and working-set demand.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: Latency spikes coincide with sustained swap-in and swap-out activity. Inspect memory demand and reduce pressure before changing swap policy.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Any configured swap proves the host is unhealthy. This is not a sound assumption; memory pressure requiring closer investigation.

lessons.takeaway: Swap activity should be correlated with latency and working-set demand.

lessons.title: Capabilities
lessons.summary: A way to split traditionally root-associated privileges.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Granting only required capabilities can reduce privilege scope.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A service only needs to bind a privileged port. Evaluate granting the narrow required capability instead of full root.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Any single capability is equivalent to no privilege. This is not a sound assumption; a way to split traditionally root-associated privileges.

lessons.takeaway: Granting only required capabilities can reduce privilege scope.

lessons.title: ACL masks
lessons.summary: It limits effective permissions for named users and the group class.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The effective ACL must be considered together with the visible entry.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: An ACL entry grants write but effective permissions show read-only. Inspect the ACL mask and intended access policy.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: The mask always grants permissions absent from the entry. This is not a sound assumption; it limits effective permissions for named users and the group class.

lessons.takeaway: The effective ACL must be considered together with the visible entry.

lessons.title: Atomic replacement
lessons.summary: Rename can atomically replace the directory entry.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Atomic visibility does not by itself guarantee durability after power loss.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: Readers sometimes see partially written configuration files. Use a validated temporary file and atomic replacement with appropriate durability handling.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Rename across arbitrary filesystems is always atomic. This is not a sound assumption; rename can atomically replace the directory entry.

lessons.takeaway: Atomic visibility does not by itself guarantee durability after power loss.

lessons.title: Namespaces
lessons.summary: Views of resources such as processes mounts and network stacks.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Namespaces are isolation mechanisms rather than resource usage budgets.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: Two containers have different interfaces but contend for host CPU. Inspect namespace isolation separately from cgroup resource controls.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: A network namespace imposes a CPU limit. This is not a sound assumption; views of resources such as processes mounts and network stacks.

lessons.takeaway: Namespaces are isolation mechanisms rather than resource usage budgets.

lessons.title: Cgroup throttling
lessons.summary: Runnable tasks can be throttled until budget becomes available.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: CPU throttling can increase latency even without host-wide CPU saturation.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A service is slow despite idle host cores and rising throttling counters. Compare CPU quota throttling and workload demand.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Quota exhaustion necessarily kills all processes immediately. This is not a sound assumption; runnable tasks can be throttled until budget becomes available.

lessons.takeaway: CPU throttling can increase latency even without host-wide CPU saturation.

lessons.title: Filesystem recovery
lessons.summary: Concurrent writes can undermine repair assumptions and risk corruption.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Recovery should follow filesystem-specific procedures and preserve evidence.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A volume reports metadata errors while applications continue writing. Protect data and arrange a controlled filesystem-specific recovery process.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Repair tools are always safe on live writable filesystems. This is not a sound assumption; concurrent writes can undermine repair assumptions and risk corruption.

lessons.takeaway: Recovery should follow filesystem-specific procedures and preserve evidence.

lessons.title: Clock selection
lessons.summary: It is not subject to wall-clock time adjustments in the same way.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Wall-clock timestamps and elapsed durations serve different purposes.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: A timeout calculation behaves strangely after a clock correction. Measure elapsed durations with the appropriate monotonic clock.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Wall-clock time can never move backward. This is not a sound assumption; it is not subject to wall-clock time adjustments in the same way.

lessons.takeaway: Wall-clock timestamps and elapsed durations serve different purposes.

lessons.title: Kernel versus user space
lessons.summary: A controlled transition from user space into kernel services.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Kernel-level faults can affect more than one application.

sections.heading: Apply it
sections.body: Several applications experience I/O failures after a kernel update. Correlate kernel and device evidence with the shared failure timeline.

sections.heading: Misconception to challenge
sections.body: Every library function requires a system call. This is not a sound assumption; a controlled transition from user space into kernel services.

lessons.takeaway: Kernel-level faults can affect more than one application.
